title: The Man Who Raised $2.4 Billion for Conservation Is Now Building a Climate Campus on a New York Island. He Is Indian American.
excerpt: Dr. M. Sanjayan, former CEO of Conservation International, will lead the New York Climate Exchange — a $250 million bet on turning Governors Island into a global hub for climate solutions.
body:
When the New York Climate Exchange needed someone to turn a vision into a building, a campus, and eventually a movement, it chose an Indian American conservation biologist who had already done something similar on a global scale.

Dr. M. Sanjayan has been named the next CEO of The New York Climate Exchange, the ambitious initiative to build a world-class climate campus on Governors Island in New York Harbor. The appointment puts one of the most prominent Indian American scientists in charge of what may become the country's most visible infrastructure project in the fight against climate change.

Sanjayan arrives with a track record that few in the climate world can match. As CEO of Conservation International from 2017 to 2025, he led two capital campaigns totaling $2.4 billion, expanded the organization to 1,800 staff across 35 countries, and forged partnerships with Apple, Microsoft, Mastercard, and Procter & Gamble. In 2024, TIME named him to its inaugural 100 Climate list.

## What the Exchange Is Building

The New York Climate Exchange is not a think tank or a foundation. It is a physical campus — a collection of buildings on Governors Island designed to bring together climate scientists, educators, entrepreneurs, and policymakers under one roof. The vision is a place where a graduate student studying sea-level rise might share a hallway with a startup building carbon-capture technology and a city planner redesigning flood-prone neighborhoods.

The project is backed by serious money: $100 million from the Simons Foundation and Simons Foundation International, $50 million from Bloomberg Philanthropies, and significant capital commitments from the City of New York. Its 48 partner institutions include some of the country's leading research universities.

Once open, the campus will host "semester abroad" style academic courses, cutting-edge research, job training for the green economy, and public programming. The Exchange's anchor institution is Stony Brook University, whose president Andrea Goldsmith chairs the board.

"Sanjayan is an exceptional leader, deeply knowledgeable scientist, and outstanding communicator," Goldsmith said. "He brings to the role an impressive track record leading transformational growth."

## A Different Kind of Indian American Success Story

The Indian American community has produced CEOs of Google, Microsoft, and IBM. It has produced senators, surgeons general, and Spelling Bee champions. But leadership in climate science and conservation has been rarer — which makes Sanjayan's appointment notable beyond the specifics of the job.

Sanjayan is a conservation biologist by training who has also become one of the most effective science communicators in the country, producing award-winning documentaries with PBS and BBC. He represents a model of Indian American achievement that does not fit neatly into the familiar boxes of tech, medicine, or finance.

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans in the United States, many of whom live in coastal cities vulnerable to climate change — New York, San Francisco, Houston, Miami — the Exchange's work is directly relevant. Climate policy shapes everything from insurance premiums to property values to the livability of the neighborhoods where the diaspora has put down roots.

## The Stakes

"Climate change is both a crisis and an opportunity for humanity," Sanjayan said in a statement. "It's a privilege to lead The New York Climate Exchange at this consequential and defining moment for people and the planet. I cannot think of a more powerful platform from which to accelerate solutions that the world urgently needs."

The campus is still under development, and the timeline for its full opening has not been announced. But with Sanjayan at the helm — a leader who has already demonstrated the ability to translate scientific urgency into institutional action and philanthropic dollars — the Exchange has signaled that it is not interested in being another climate conference venue. It wants to be the place where the solutions actually get built.

For an Indian American scientist who spent eight years convincing the world's largest companies to invest in conservation, that might be exactly the right next challenge.
